correctness.rationale: Multiplicativity gives Δ=(3+3p−p²)q+3(p²+p+1). Also σ(n)/n≤(3/2)(13/9)(6/5)=13/5<3, so an omitted divisor cannot equal n. For p≥7 the negative q-coefficient and q≥p+2 give the bound −p³+4p²+12p+9, negative at 7 and strictly decreasing thereafter. For p=5, Δ=93−7q and Δ≥3 force q∈{7,11}. For p=3 the divisor split is A∪qB with A={1,2,3,6,9,18}, B={1,2,3,6,9}; for q≥17, two A terms are too small, mixed pairs are either below 3q+39 (b≤3) or above it (b≥6), and two qB terms require q|39. The q=13 boundary has no two distinct B coefficients summing to 6, and no mixed or A-only witnesses. Independently scanning the divisors d=1,…,n and testing d<Δ−d and (Δ−d)|n reproduced the unique pairs for 90,126,198,550 and no pairs for 234,350,650. The proof, not the finite scan, gives the unbounded classification.
residual_risks: The packaged 4,371-pair regression was not rerun and is not needed for the exclusion proof.
Exactly two distinct omitted divisors and p<q are essential to the assessed statement.

originality.rationale: A distinct indexed theorem classifies all 2-near-perfect integers with three distinct prime factors and four prime factors with multiplicity. Restricting its list to the repeated smaller odd prime gives exactly the four frozen values and exactly the same omissions. The records share a date; this is demonstrable statement-level coverage, not a conclusion about chronology, independent discovery or direction of dependence. The earlier examples and OEIS alone would not justify this decision.
residual_risks: Same-day dates and the broader record's attribution do not establish which construction was obtained first.
The external search does not prove absence of another broader classification; the inspected result already establishes coverage.
